MMInA: Benchmarking Multihop Multimodal Internet Agents

1,050 human-written tasks chain across up to ten evolving, real-world websites — Wikipedia to a flight search to a hotel booking to YouTube — each requiring an agent to combine images and text across multiple hops. GPT-4V, the paper's headline multimodal model, clears only 21.8% of tasks end-to-end against a 96.3% human ceiling.

// citation count as of 2026-07
// the gap

What problem is this solving?

By 2024, web-agent benchmarks had started to take multimodality seriously — VisualWebArena (Koh et al., 2024) added images to WebArena's text-only environment — but almost none of them asked an agent to leave a single website. WebArena's tasks average 1.06 hops per task (max 2); VisualWebArena, 1.05 (max 2); Mind2Web, exactly 1.00 across all 131 sites it covers; even RUSS, at 1.10 hops, barely leaves the starting page. MMInA's authors are blunt about why this matters: "we found that the tasks of existing benchmarks are oversimplified whose completions requiring a single website, which is highly diverged from the natural web browsing tasks." A real user task routinely looks like "which city has a Ferris wheel at its center, Seoul or Tianjin — book me a flight there, a hotel, and find some YouTube videos of the city" — a chain of lookups and actions across four unrelated sites, several of which require reading an image (a wheel, a room photo, a product swatch) rather than just parsing HTML.

MMInA targets that gap directly: 1,050 human-written tasks spanning 14 evolving, real-world websites, averaging 2.85 hops per task (the longest task takes 10 hops) and 12.9 actions to complete. Every task requires processing both visual and textual page content, and — unlike WebArena's or VisualWebArena's mostly-static self-hosted sites — MMInA runs against live, changing pages (Wikipedia via a dated Kiwix mirror, momondo, trip.com, Twitter, YouTube, and others), with only the shopping site (an offline OneStopMarket clone) kept static.

// how it works

The method

MMInA follows WebArena's formulation of web browsing as a POMDP ⟨S, A, P, R⟩: the state space is the entire internet plus browser/agent status, too large to represent directly, so the agent instead receives a partial observation — an accessibility tree (a structured, pruned view of page content) with any embedded images downloaded and each image's element ID painted directly onto it, so a multimodal agent can reference a specific picture by ID. The action space is a fixed set of 12 summarized actions (click, scroll, type, and so on), executed via the Playwright library on an X graphics server. One hop is defined as one subtask completed on a single website; the environment issues a PASS/FAIL for each hop as the agent moves through the chain.

The 1,050 tasks were built two ways: GPT-4V was prompted to generate WebQA-style multimodal questions (108 of the final QA pairs are adapted directly from the WebQA dataset), and three human annotators — varying in age and gender, trained on shared guidelines — manually authored additional tasks to diversify style and domain, acting as "omniscient readers" who solve each task via its shortest valid path and record every website node that path touches; all annotations were then cross-validated. Altogether the tasks combine 2,989 hops (Figure 2's own donut chart rounds this to 2,991) across Wikipedia, an offline shopping site, flight/hotel/car-rental/train booking, event search, Twitter, YouTube, food discovery, currency exchange, a travel-guide site, and recipes — Wikipedia alone supplies 28.4% of hops, shopping 13.0%, flight 10.5%, hotel 10.3%, and car rental 9.2%, with the remaining domains each under 8%. By intent, 64.7% of hops are action hops (book, purchase, navigate) and 35.3% are information-seeking (look something up).

MMInA scores agents with two distinct metrics that are not interchangeable. Single-hop evaluation uses either must_include — a strict, keyword-based check where every required keyword must appear in the agent's answer — or fuzzy_match, a lenient LLM-judged check (GPT-3.5-Turbo is asked "Given the statement pred, would it be correct to infer reference? Yes or No") that tolerates paraphrase, e.g. accepting "gold" for a reference answer of "yellow." Multihop evaluation maintains an ordered queue of per-hop completion conditions plus a terminal "END" marker (queue length N+1 for an N-hop task); the agent can only advance to hop k+1 once hop k's condition — reaching a target URL or producing a target string — is verified, and a task is credited as fully solved only if every hop completes correctly, in sequence.

hop SR (%) = 100 × successful hop-level visitstotal hops evaluated // granular, partial credit — a model can score well here while finishing almost no full tasks
task SR (%) = 100 × tasks with every hop completed, in ordertotal tasks // strict, all-or-nothing — this is the metric quoted in the paper's introduction

To address the resulting multihop collapse (see Results), the paper proposes a lightweight memory-augmented agent built from three memory types: semantic memory (the model's general world knowledge, baked into its weights), episodic memory (the in-context action trajectory for the task currently being solved), and procedural memory (the recorded action sequence and outcome of past, similar, already-completed tasks). Concretely, the agent's prompt is augmented with the K most similar past task trajectories before it acts; the authors find K=2 near-optimal empirically — smaller histories (K=1–2) work best on simpler domains like shopping or Wikipedia, while larger histories add length and bias without a compensating benefit.

// what they found

The results

The authors evaluate three families of agents — text-only LLMs reading the accessibility tree, the same text-only LLMs augmented with BLIP-2-generated image captions, and true multimodal LMMs that see the images directly — plus WebShop as a web-trained heuristic baseline and a human baseline averaged over 3 test-takers. GPT-4V, the strongest genuinely multimodal model, reaches an overall task success rate of 21.77% (reported as "21.8%" in the introduction) and an overall hop success rate of 13.89%. Humans reach 96.25% overall task SR and 98.43% overall hop SR (the introduction rounds this to "96.3%") — every one of the eighteen non-human agent rows in the results table trails the human row in every column, hop-level and task-level alike, and the gap widens sharply with hop count: at 5+ hops, the best agent's task SR is a mere 1.13%, reached by both Gemini-Pro-Vision configurations (plain and history-augmented), against 88.12% for humans on the same slice.

Multihop tasks are not simply harder versions of single-hop tasks — they collapse almost entirely. At the aggregated 2–4 hop band, the best task SR among all tested agents is the history-augmented Gemini-Pro-Vision's 10.61%, just ahead of GPT-4's text-only 9.09%; at 5+ hops, fifteen of the eighteen agent rows record exactly 0% task SR, with only three nonzero entries — both Gemini-Pro-Vision configurations at 1.13% and caption-augmented Gemini-Pro at 0.38%. The hop-level breakdown in Table 3 shows why: for both GPT-4V and Gemini-Pro-Vision, first-hop success falls sharply as a task's total hop count grows — GPT-4V's first-hop SR drops from 56.50% on 2-hop tasks to 22.73% on 3-hop tasks (Gemini-Pro-Vision: 69.28% → 32.56%) — and from the third hop onward, both models score exactly 0.00% in every hop-count bucket the table reports (H.C. 2 through 6). The paper attributes the early-hop decay itself to an enlarged search space and weak zero-shot long-context reasoning, compounded by agents that "wander" into unrelated sites once under-informed rather than persistently retrying the correct one.

The memory-augmented agent (built on Gemini-Pro-Vision) improves on this baseline: with history length K=2, overall performance rises from roughly 15 (K=0, no memory) to about 22, and 1-hop performance from about 29 to about 39 — the largest gains are concentrated in the 1-hop and 2–4-hop bands, while the 5+-hop band stays close to the floor regardless of K, since a task that already fails deep in the chain has little trajectory history to draw on.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

MMInA's core design choices are sound: real, live websites instead of frozen HTML snapshots make memorization-based shortcuts harder, and splitting hop-level from task-level success is a genuinely useful diagnostic — it's exactly what exposes that agents aren't merely "a bit worse" on long chains, they are failing completely past the second hop. But one of the paper's own three headline claims doesn't survive a close read of its own Table 2. The "Multimodality-reliance" bullet states multimodal models show "overall higher performance in both hop and task performance" — yet the single best non-human result in the entire results table is DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B in the caption-augmented (text) setting, at 23.07% overall task SR, which beats the paper's own best true-multimodal model, GPT-4V, at 21.77%. A second counter-example sits within the GPT-4 family itself: GPT-4's caption-augmented text run reaches 19.85% overall task SR, while GPT-4o — genuinely multimodal — manages only 11.61–14.04% across its two tested configurations, trailing that caption-only run. This isn't a wholesale rebuttal of the multimodality claim — the GPT-4 lineage's own multimodal headline row (GPT-4V, 21.77%) does exceed its caption-augmented run (9.34% text → 19.85% caption → 21.77% GPT-4V is monotone), and Gemini-Pro (9.54% text → 15.22% caption → 18.40–20.13% Gemini-Pro-Vision) and Fuyu-8B (0% text → 13.39% multimodal) show the same increasing pattern the paper claims. But a blanket "multimodal models do better" reading of this benchmark is still not fully warranted: the single best non-human score anywhere in the table is a text-based, caption-augmented model outscoring every multimodal row, and both of GPT-4o's tested configurations trail the caption-augmented GPT-4 baseline — a different checkpoint (Appendix A.1 pins them to gpt-4o-2024-11-20 and gpt-4-0125-preview), so this is a comparison within the GPT-4 lineage rather than a controlled same-model ablation.

baselines

Three input settings (text-only, caption-augmented, true multimodal) plus a real 3-tester human baseline is a fair comparison in principle, but the paper's own numbers show a caption-augmented text model (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, 23.07% overall task SR) outscoring every true multimodal model including its own headline GPT-4V (21.77%) — undercutting the "multimodality helps" framing stated in the results discussion.

contamination

Running on live, evolving sites (Wikipedia, momondo, trip.com, Twitter, YouTube) is a real anti-memorization design choice, but it cuts both ways: because most reference sites are dynamic, a ground-truth answer recorded at annotation time (a flight price, a hotel's availability, a tweet) can go stale by the time an agent is evaluated, and the paper reports no re-verification step or estimate of how much near-zero multihop performance reflects environment drift rather than agent failure.

what's missed

The main-text hop-by-hop table (Table 3) only tabulates hop counts 2–6, even though tasks run up to 10 hops; the appendix's fuller breakdown (Table A1, GPT-4V only) shows first-hop success actually climbing back up for 7–10-hop tasks (e.g. 56.67% at 9 hops) rather than continuing to decline — a reversal the paper attributes to small sample sizes (19–59 tasks per bucket — 59/35/30/19 for the 7/8/9/10-hop buckets) without further investigation, and the main text never surfaces this caveat.

would raise confidence

A re-verification pass confirming task ground truths hadn't gone stale between annotation and each model's evaluation run; a quantified breakdown of first-hop failures by cause (the paper's own "wandering" explanation is currently anecdotal, not measured); and extending Table 3's heatmap to the full 2–10 hop range in the main text, with the appendix's small-n caveat stated alongside it rather than left in Appendix A.3.

// bottom line

MMInA is a real advance in benchmark realism — genuine cross-site chains on live websites, with a hop-vs-task success split that cleanly exposes how completely current agents fail past the second hop of a task. But its own results table complicates its "multimodality helps" narrative more than the paper's discussion admits, and its headline "agents fail earlier as tasks get longer" story is built mainly on the 2–6-hop range; the 7–10-hop appendix data doesn't clearly continue that trend, on samples too small to settle the question either way.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. MMInA chains 1,050 human-written tasks across 14 evolving, real-world websites, averaging 2.85 hops (up to 10) and 12.9 actions per task — a genuine step up in compositionality from single-site benchmarks like WebArena (1.06 avg. hops) and VisualWebArena (1.05 avg. hops).
  2. It separates a granular hop success rate (per-website credit) from a strict task success rate (the full chain, in order); by the latter, GPT-4V's 21.8% badly trails the 96.3% human ceiling, and both GPT-4V and Gemini-Pro-Vision score exactly 0.00% on the third hop or later, at every hop count Table 3 reports.
  3. The paper's own results complicate its "multimodality helps" headline: the single best non-human score anywhere in the table (23.07% overall task SR) comes from a caption-augmented text model, not a true multimodal one — a memory-augmented agent (K=2 past trajectories) still helps the most on 1-hop and mid-length tasks, but barely moves the near-zero 5+-hop floor.
